Natalie’s rebellion—drunken binges, junk food, and estrangement from friends—reveals her growing disillusionment, yet she remains trapped in a cycle of ‘fallow periods’ between pregnancies. The novel contrasts with Caro Claire Burke’s *Yesteryear*, another debut about a tradwife influencer, by exploring the intersection of corporate control and personal identity. In the end, Natalie’s journey culminates in a feminist commune, suggesting that her prolonged ‘fallow’ period may have paved the way for self-discovery. Anderson’s sharp prose critiques the tech industry’s relentless pursuit of efficiency, framing motherhood as both a biological necessity and a corporate asset, while questioning the feasibility of ‘having it all’ in a world that reduces life to measurable output.

item.title: Turkey’s investment-fund fiasco
item.description:
Source: The Economist - Finance & Economics
Turkey's stock market collapsed after a burst bubble in investment funds that had previously delivered astronomical returns. Dozens of funds, including Tera (which saw its main fund rise over 60,000% in three years) and Destek Finans Faktoring (which surged 7,000% in 17 months), collapsed as investors sought to withdraw their money. The market regulator liquidated 131 funds holding $18bn in assets, leaving at least 450,000 investors facing significant losses. Authorities arrested scores of finance executives, including Tera’s chairman, on fraud charges, and froze assets of others. The scandal triggered a 5% drop in Turkey’s main stock index, wiping $30bn from the market in two days. The collapse followed years of regulatory warnings, including from Finance Minister Mehmet Simsek, who had flagged market manipulation and called for stricter rules. MSCI had warned Turkey risked being downgraded to a frontier market if regulators failed to act. Despite these signals, regulators delayed responses, only imposing restrictions in late August, which led to a sharp market sell-off. Critics, including a former financial-crimes watchdog official, claimed they were ignored or threatened with legal action for raising alarms. Simsek downplayed the crisis as isolated incidents, but analysts argue the scandal reflects deeper issues, including political influence over some firms. The fallout undermines Turkey’s ambitions to become a global financial hub and has shaken investor confidence. Inflation, which exceeded 80% in 2022 and remains around 30% annually, has driven many to seek high returns in equities, often with disastrous results. The crisis highlights systemic risks in Turkey’s financial system, with investors now facing losses after chasing unrealistic gains. Analysts warn that addressing regulatory delays and political interference is critical to restoring trust, but such steps appear unlikely. The scandal also underscores the broader economic challenges facing Turkey, where soaring prices have eroded consumer confidence and exposed vulnerabilities in its financial markets.

item.title: Good Villains Are Hard to Come By. This One’s Great.
item.description:
Source: The Atlantic - Culture
Madeline ffitch’s novel *Avalon, Rise* reimagines the classic good-versus-evil narrative through the lens of contemporary Appalachian life, offering a nuanced exploration of resistance against white nationalism. Set in a small Ohio town loosely based on Athens, the story follows a group of marginalized characters confronting Stasia, a neo-Nazi who moves to Avalon and spreads her extremist ideology. Unlike traditional villains, Stasia is portrayed as a complex figure with a following, forcing the townspeople to grapple with both external threats and internal divisions. The novel draws inspiration from children’s literature, particularly *Abiyoyo*, a tale about a boy and his father saving their village from a giant, which ffitch adapts to symbolize the fight against systemic evil. Key characters include Woody, a recovering addict and printmaker whose artistic aspirations and vulnerability to manipulation drive much of the plot, and Eloise, a well-meaning librarian whose desire to avoid conflict inadvertently enables Stasia’s influence. The story also centers on Emma, a mother struggling with her own failings, including physical abuse of her son, Martin. ffitch balances moral clarity with emotional complexity, avoiding preachiness by focusing on the messy, often futile efforts of ordinary people to resist oppression. The novel’s strength lies in its refusal to simplify good and evil, instead highlighting the difficulty of collective action and the personal costs of resistance. By weaving together themes of addiction, community, and moral ambiguity, *Avalon, Rise* challenges modern literary trends that shy away from clear villains, offering a sophisticated, morally grounded narrative that echoes the enduring power of children’s stories to inspire courage in the face of darkness.

item.title: The Powerful Yet Fragile Force Propping Up Stocks and the Economy
item.description:
Source: NYT > Your Money
The article discusses how the artificial intelligence (A.I.) industry is a critical but fragile force supporting the stock market and broader economy despite rising interest rates and bond market turmoil. While bond yields have hit their highest level since 2002, the stock market and economy remain resilient, partly due to A.I.'s rapid growth. The iShares U.S. Technology ETF, a proxy for A.I.-led tech stocks, returned 35.2% in 2024, far outperforming the S&P 500 Ex-Technology ETF’s 4.4%. Mark Zandi, chief economist at Moody’s Analytics, estimates A.I. contributed 0.6–0.7 percentage points to U.S. GDP growth in the second quarter of 2024, potentially accounting for 30% of inflation-adjusted economic growth. However, this reliance on A.I. is precarious. Concerns about A.I. safety have intensified, with Evan Hubinger of Anthropic warning the chance A.I. could 'kill all humans' within a decade exceeds 10%. A.I. companies and leaders are calling for regulatory 'guardrails' to ensure safety, but President Trump dismisses these concerns as a 'hoax,' fearing a slowdown could trigger a stock market crash and recession. Analysts warn the A.I. stock boom may be nearing its end, with Capital Economics suggesting a market bubble could burst by late 2025. The S&P 500’s concentration in tech stocks—10 companies now account for over 40% of its market cap—heightens risks. A.I. also drives economic growth through the 'wealth effect,' boosting consumer spending, and massive infrastructure investments, with Goldman Sachs projecting $1 trillion in global A.I. spending by 2026 and Columbia professor Stijn Van Nieuwerburgh estimating $10.3 trillion in U.S. capital expenditures by 2032. However, rising bond yields and debt financing for A.I. projects could strain the economy. While the A.I. boom has fueled stock gains, its collapse could devastate markets and the broader economy, prompting investors to consider bonds and high-yield savings as safer alternatives amid uncertainty.

item.title: Carrie, With Kid Gloves
item.description:
Source: The Atlantic - Culture
The article discusses the TV adaptation of Stephen King’s 1974 novel *Carrie*, adapted by showrunner Mike Flanagan for Prime Video. The original story follows Carrie White, a high school student tormented by her religious mother and bullies, who unleashes telekinetic powers during her prom after being doused in pig’s blood, destroying her town in a fit of vengeance. The novel, published in 1974 amid Cold War paranoia, is known for blurring the line between victim and villain. Flanagan’s adaptation modernizes the story, setting it in the present day and incorporating social media as a tool for the characters’ actions. The series stars Summer H. Howell as Carrie and explores how technology amplifies the teenagers’ impulses. However, the show is criticized for being overly empathetic to its characters, portraying them as victims of systemic forces rather than allowing them to revel in their cruelty as in the source material. This approach removes the catharsis of Carrie’s climactic revenge, which was central to the original novel’s impact. The adaptation’s focus on modern issues like surveillance and shame contrasts with the 1974 book’s portrayal of a paranoid, pre-digital world. While some modernizations are praised for relevance, the show’s handling of the characters’ vindictiveness has drawn mixed reactions, with some arguing it dilutes the original’s tragic intensity.

item.title: The Decade’s 10 Most Defining Movies (So Far)
item.description:
Source: The Atlantic - Culture
This article presents a list of 10 films deemed defining of the 2020s, curated by David Sims in his newsletter Video Village. The decade’s cinematic landscape is framed as an atmospheric reflection of Hollywood’s evolution, shaped by the pandemic, streaming dominance, and industry shifts. Two standout releases are Greta Gerwig’s *Barbie* (2023) and Christopher Nolan’s *Oppenheimer* (2023), which premiered during a labor strike and pandemic recovery, sparking a multibillion-dollar cultural phenomenon. Other films highlight the era’s themes: Spike Lee’s *Da 5 Bloods* (2020) intertwines Vietnam War history with contemporary American struggles, while Joachim Trier’s *The Worst Person in the World* (2021) explores a 30-year-old’s existential uncertainties. Ryusuke Hamaguchi’s *Drive My Car* (2021), a three-hour Japanese drama, became an Oscar nominee and is praised for its emotional depth. Todd Field’s *Tár* (2022) examines ego and power through a conductor’s unraveling, while Jordan Peele’s *Nope* (2022) critiques entertainment industry exploitation with its flying monster metaphor. S. S. Rajamouli’s *RRR* (2022) revitalized grand-scale action filmmaking, and Wes Anderson’s *Asteroid City* (2023) offers a darkly comedic take on quarantine-era isolation. Recent entries include Pascal Plante’s *Red Rooms* (2024), a horror film about online obsession, and Ari Aster’s *Eddington* (2025), which explores pandemic-era online toxicity. The article also mentions Kane Parsons’ *Backrooms* (2026), a horror film directed by a young filmmaker, and notes the enduring legacy of *Carrie*’s iconic climax. The list underscores how cinema has mirrored the decade’s cultural and societal shifts, from streaming’s rise to mental health struggles and digital-age anxieties.

item.title: The Reporter Who Exposed Elizabeth Holmes on Nathan Fielder’s Documentary
item.description:
Source: NYT > Business
The article details the experience of a former Wall Street Journal reporter who investigated Elizabeth Holmes and her company Theranos, which was later exposed as a fraud. The reporter recounts how Holmes denied interviews and used legal threats to silence critics, including dispatching David Boies to intimidate them. The reporter’s findings, which concluded Holmes’s claims about Theranos’s blood-testing technology were false, were later chronicled in the author’s book, 'Bad Blood.' The article focuses on the documentary 'You Can See Everything,' directed by Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim, which grants Holmes a platform to defend herself after her 2022 conviction for defrauding investors and a 11-year prison sentence. The reporter reflects on their interactions with Fielder, noting how Holmes’s attempts to portray herself as misunderstood and neurodivergent were undermined by her dishonesty, such as her inability to grasp the humor in the Abbott and Costello sketch. The film also highlights Holmes’s emotional breakdown during a photo session with her partner, Billy Evans, and her denial of wrongdoing, which the reporter contrasts with the judge’s observation that fraud often involves a refusal to accept responsibility. The article also touches on Evans’s alliance with Ryan El-Hosseiny, a self-promoter who claims to have rebuilt Theranos’s technology and publicly defended Holmes’s innocence despite evidence of the company’s failures. The reporter emphasizes how the documentary exposes Holmes’s contradictions, from her past embrace of media attention to her current desperate attempts to control her narrative, underscoring the broader cautionary tale of her fraud.

item.title: What Aaron Sorkin Forgot About The Social Network
item.description:
Source: The Atlantic - Culture
Aaron Sorkin’s sequel to *The Social Network*, *The Social Reckoning*, dramatizes Facebook’s role in societal harm through the lens of investigative journalist Jeff Horwitz and whistleblower Frances Haugen. Set between 2019 and 2021, the film is based on Wall Street Journal articles exposing Facebook’s algorithmic amplification of harmful content. Sorkin’s work is praised for its public good but criticized for its lack of excitement and emotional depth compared to the original film. The narrative focuses on Horwitz’s collaboration with Haugen to reveal the company’s misdeeds, though their dynamic lacks the tumultuous interpersonal tension seen in the original’s portrayal of Zuckerberg and Eduardo Saverin’s rivalry. Sorkin’s direction is deemed flat, with muted visuals and static settings that contrast with David Fincher’s evocative portrayal of Harvard in *The Social Network*. Zuckerberg is reimagined by Jeremy Strong, who portrays the CEO as stiff and unengaging, a departure from Jesse Eisenberg’s nuanced, youthful performance. The film’s structure, which jumps between time periods including the coronavirus pandemic and the January 6 insurrection, is criticized as choppy and unfocused. While Sorkin’s script highlights Facebook’s role in fostering hate and misinformation, the film’s reliance on tired screenwriting tropes and its failure to engage with topical issues in an interesting way diminish its impact. Despite its factual accuracy, *The Social Reckoning* is seen as a perfunctory follow-up that lacks the poetic urgency of its predecessor.

item.title: How to survive a predatory world order
item.description:
Source: The Economist - International
Middle powers face growing threats from dominant nations like the U.S., China, and Russia, prompting calls for unity. In a January 2024 speech at the World Economic Forum, Canada’s Prime Minister Justin Trudeau (Mark Carney) urged middle-ranked countries to form coalitions to resist bullying by superpowers. He warned that the old rules-based international order no longer constrains the powerful, leaving smaller nations vulnerable. Carney’s speech reflected Canada’s own struggles under U.S. President Donald Trump’s economic pressure, including tariffs and threats to invade Greenland. While some middle powers have resisted, such as Denmark’s support for Greenland and Japan’s refusal to apologize for criticizing China’s potential attack on Taiwan, others remain hesitant. The article highlights the fragmented nature of middle powers, with differing priorities and definitions of who qualifies as such. For example, countries like Brazil, India, and South Africa question Canada’s leadership in reshaping the global order. Meanwhile, the U.S.-China relationship has shifted toward cooperation, complicating efforts by middle powers to challenge both. Trump’s pragmatic approach to China, including trade deals and avoiding conflict, has created a fragile truce, though tensions persist. The article notes that middle powers face a dilemma: aligning with one superpower risks provoking the other. Singapore’s Lee Kuan Yew warned that both U.S.-China rivalry and collusion endanger smaller nations. Despite some successes, such as the EU’s resistance to China’s trade pressures, middle powers struggle to act collectively. The article concludes that while Carney’s call for unity is urgent, the lack of consensus and the shifting dynamics between superpowers make it difficult for middle powers to navigate a predatory global order.

item.title: Mirror life is dangerous. Regulators must act before it becomes real
item.description:
Source: The Economist - Leaders
Mirror life, a form of synthetic biology where organic molecules exist in reversed handedness compared to natural life, poses significant risks if created. Scientists warn that artificial cells with mirror molecules could evade immune detection, become highly pathogenic, and disrupt ecosystems by evading natural predators like viruses and amoebas. While potential benefits include drug development, the dangers outweigh these possibilities. The article emphasizes the urgency of regulatory action, as synthetic biology advances rapidly with AI assistance, enabling the creation of entirely new biochemistries. Unlike past technologies, there is still time to implement safeguards. The piece calls for global cooperation, including banning funding and research into mirror life, monitoring suspicious orders for synthetic molecules, and imposing guardrails on AI models to prevent misuse. Biosurveillance tests would also be needed to detect mirror life in the environment. While rational actors or corporations are unlikely to pursue mirror life due to its uncontrollable risks, irrational actors like cults could pose a threat. The article references the 1970s Asilomar conference on genetic engineering as a historical precedent but argues that today’s globalized, profit-driven biotech landscape requires stronger measures. China’s growing role in biotechnology is highlighted as a critical factor. The conclusion stresses that proactive regulation is essential to prevent unintended consequences, as humanity must address known threats before confronting unknown future risks.

item.title: Inheritances Can Shatter Families. Could a Therapist Help?
item.description:
Source: NYT > Your Money
Bill Martin, a 55-year-old farmer in Oregon, wants his three sons to maintain the close family bonds he and his brother lost after their father’s retirement in 2022. The brothers, now estranged, clashed over managing the family farm, leading to a breakdown in their relationship. To prevent his sons from repeating the same mistakes, Martin hired a coach-therapist to help create a succession plan prioritizing family harmony. Over the next two decades, the U.S. will see an estimated $124 trillion in wealth transfers from boomers to younger generations, often sparking family conflict. Experts like Donna Hillier, a Florida psychologist, emphasize that inheritance disputes are not just about money but about identity, legacy, and perceived fairness. Hillier notes that therapists help families develop the capacity to disagree without letting conflict erode relationships. Nancy Burgoyne, a psychologist at Northwestern University, adds that inheritors often grapple with questions of worth, such as whether they were favored over siblings. Therapists encourage parents to communicate their reasoning for decisions, even when outcomes can’t satisfy everyone, to foster respect and reduce resentment. Elaine Froese, a Canadian farm coach, has guided over 1,400 families through succession planning, stressing the importance of addressing emotional dynamics before legal and financial details. Martin’s brother, Doug, regrets not seeking such guidance earlier, as their family’s rift has strained relationships with their aging parents. Martin’s son Max appreciates his father’s efforts to avoid repeating past mistakes. Experts argue that while accountants and lawyers handle logistics, therapists and coaches focus on communication and conflict resolution, helping families navigate the emotional complexities of inheritance.

item.title: Black Unemployment Hints at a Job Market in Worse Shape Than It Seems
item.description:
Source: NYT > Business
Black unemployment rates have risen sharply, signaling deeper labor market struggles than suggested by overall national figures. Gena Pemberton, a Black woman who lost her job at Omnicom Health in 2025, has been unemployed for over a year despite extensive job searches. Her experience reflects a broader crisis: Black professionals face a 'triple whammy' of lost diversity, equity, and inclusion (D.E.I.) roles; federal job cuts that disproportionately affected Black workers; and slower white-collar hiring. Black unemployment hit 7% in September 2025, double the 3.6% rate for white workers, with Black women bearing the brunt of job losses. Data shows Black women’s employment dropped to 10.3 million from a 2023 peak, while Black men’s employment fell but partially recovered. Experts like Jared Bernstein warn that the labor market’s struggles mirror the post-2008 recession, with Black unemployment remaining elevated. Federal government job cuts and reduced support for Black entrepreneurship have exacerbated challenges, as seen in Melinda Emerson’s experience with canceled contracts and slashed budgets. AI-driven hiring practices have also marginalized Black professionals, favoring old-school networks that many lack. While some optimism exists—such as Cantrell Dumas noting Black labor force participation remains strong—many Black workers, like Pemberton, face financial strain, with some tapping into retirement savings. The decline of D.E.I. initiatives and corporate shifts toward exclusionary practices have deepened disparities, leaving many struggling to find stable employment.
